Harold Davis

Harold Davis

Harold Davis  

Psychoanalysis as an Intellectual Discipline is the first of two volumes containing the proceedings of the conference in 1981 on “The Vital Issues” that commemorated fifty years of organized psychoanalysis in Chicago. The book covers four aspects of psychoanalysis as an intellectual discipline. Part 1 on the origin of motivation deals with its roots in neurobiology, with developmental psychology and with the complex question of the use of data from infant observation. The problem of interdisciplinary collaboration is considered in the second part with examples presented from social science. Part 3 focuses on creativity and the course of human life. The epistemology of psychoanalysis is the subject of the final part. The authors include humanist-scholars David Bevington, Mark Schwehn and Mary Gedo and social scientists Donald Levine, Melford Spiro and Waud Kracke together with psychoanalytic thinkers Michael Basch, David Freedman, Mark Gehrie, Arnold Goldberg, William Grossman, Joseph Lichtenberg, George Moraitis, Henri Parens, Barbara Rocah, Leo Sadow, Samuel Weiss and the editors, John Gedo and George Pollock.

Volume II, Clinical Psychoanalysis and Its Applications, explores unsolved problems in the clinical theory of psychoanalysis, both in and outside of the therapeutic setting. Five sections deal with logically related topics—Transference and Countertransference, Self Psychology and its Alternatives, Outcome Studies, Theoretical Problems and Applications in the Literary Realm. An epilogue recounts the history of psychoanalysis in Chicago.

Ping-Nie Pao was, for fifteen years until his death in 1981, Director of Psychotherapy at Chestnut Lodge, in a suburb of Washington, D.C., where interest in schizophrenia and work with schizophrenics has been a tradition since Frieda Fromm-Reichmann's stay as its first director of psychotherapy. Ping-Nie Pao's views on schizophrenia are consistent with those of Fromm-Reichmann and also with those of Chestnut Lodge's other most famous worker, Harold Searles. “I conceptualize schizophrenia in terms of human development; that is, a certain combination of nature and nurture in the first weeks of life results in a poor tolerance of affective experience and a deficient capacity for adaptation, which becomes increasingly worse and eventuates in schizophrenic illness.” (This from his comprehensive book, Schizophrenic Disorders.) This present collection of essays grew out of a conference held at Chestnut Lodge to honor and further Ping-Nie Pao's contribution to this area of psychoanalytic thought. Among the international contributors are Vamik Volkan, Joseph and Anne-Marie Sandler, James S. Grotstein, Clarice Kestenbaum.

Eighty years after publication of Freud's revelations concerning infantile sexuality, many schools of therapeutic thought have moved so far away from his original insights that Herbert S. Strean's book is a necessary corrective to the tendency to treat sexual dysfunctions without consideration of their psychodynamic and historical context. Strean provides seventy case examples of sexual conflicts and anxieties in clients of all ages. Furthermore, he shows, in the tradition of Freud's tracing of the vicissitudes of instinctual impulses, how underlying sexual disorders can be the basis for ostensibly nonsexual problems, phobias, addictions, passivities, etc. Strean provides a variety of assessment skills and therapies to guide helping professionals, from nurses to psychoanalysts, in their treatment of psychosexual problems.

Howard Ruttenberg

Howard Ruttenberg

Howard Ruttenberg  

This is a collection of essays by the famous anti-psychiatry psychiatrist, written over the past twenty-five years, on a variety of topics focused on current events, collected under eight headings such as Mental Illness, Mental Health Policy, The Insanity Defense, Psychiatry and Politics, etc. Szasz comments, often in only a few pages, on psychosurgery, involuntary hospitalization, electroshock, the Tylenol poisonings, Dan White, Hinckley, Martha Mitchell, Jim Jones, Ezra Pound, Soviet psychiatry, drug education and prohibition, and sex education, from a point of view that denies that mental illness exists and that regards the concept of mental illness as part of an ideology that has largely replaced moral and religious thinking. Because this ideology goes unrecognized as such, since it parades as science, Szasz contends, it not only usurps the role of moral deliberation, it oversteps the juridical limitations placed upon creeds for the sake of protecting individual rights.

Although his arguments are directed specifically against psychiatry, the ideology he attacks clearly includes psychoanalysis as well, even when the analysand freely elects to engage in it. Szasz raises basic questions about what it means to be mentally ill and to be cured that receive different answers from analysts who disagree on the relation between psychoanalysis and medicine and biology. Whatever the progress of this debate may be, Szasz performs an important function in helping analysts and analysands to recognize moral and political issues, not only in medical terms like “cure” but also in more favored psychoanalytic ones such as “good functioning,” “ego strength,” etc.

Drive theorists will be helped by Szasz's polemic to recognize that their therapy is a moral theory, albeit one based on biological assumptions.

The Hermeneutics Reader: Texts of the German Tradition from the Enlightenment to the Present. Kurt Mueller-Vollmer, editor. New York: The Continuum Publishing Company, 1985. 345 pp.

Howard Ruttenberg

Howard Ruttenberg

Howard Ruttenberg  

While English-speaking philosophers have, for the most part, tested psychoanalysis against the standards of experimental science,

135

on the continent philosophy has often embraced psychoanalysis but in theoretical terms and meanings scarcely recognizable, at least to the American practitioner. Many writers in the continental tradition have recently had their works classed as “hermeneutics;” this text seeks to clarify that term by tracing its use by German philosophers from the 18th, but principally in the last two centuries, in a variety of fields of study, including philosophy, history, philology, theology, and the social sciences. In its first phase, hermeneutics is philological, concerned with the interpretation of texts. In the second and contemporary phase its scope and meaning are widened to include the whole of philosophy. This expansion is due to seminal thinkers such as Dilthey and Husserl, and is, like the variety of phenomenologies to which they gave rise, the result of a shift in focus away from the abstractions of ideas and theories and toward the concreteness of what men say and do. That all psychic processes can be regarded as symbolic presentations is perhaps an idea that Freud owed to his teacher Brentano, who is not represented in this text except through another of his illustrious students, Husserl. But the hermeneutic tradition may be characterized in terms of opting for the opposite of Freud's choice of interpreting psychic symbols as reflections of biological drives. Instead, they view the hermeneutic process as constitutive, rather than merely reflective of individual history and character. It is this notion of personal meaning that has led psychoanalysts inspired by this tradition to give up the quest for reconstruction of the analysand's past, on the general grounds that what was meaningul to one and no longer is so is no longer of concern. From this brief indication of what the hermeneutic thinkers are up to, it is perhaps clear that understanding them can help us understand continental analysts such as Lacan, whose thought merged their insights with those of Freud, and it can help us to understand some modern innovations on Freudian thought, such as the idea of the liberating life story.

Editors' Introduction

With this issue, Modern Psychoanalysis begins its second decade of publication. To mark the completion of the first decade, the editors have included a complete list of the contents pages of each issue since we began publication. We hope this will help new readers to find which back issues would be of interest to them. We have also included an alphabetical index, by author, of all the articles published to date. This index should make it easier for those who are interested in particular authors to find their work.

Over these past ten years we have witnessed the modern analytic approach to dealing with preoedipal disorders being utilized more and more by those who are trained and are seeking training. This influence and acceptance have been gratifying. In the next decade we look forward to continuing to publish papers reflecting current research and demonstrating how analysis has been developing in response to patient treatment.

Estelle Borowitz

Estelle Borowitz  

For some years now, Gedo has been interested in constructing a “maximally inclusive and relevant clinical theory.” This book, the sixth in a series, completes his effort in this regard by contrasting his views and “their applications in the treatment setting” with

118

the views of others who have been engaged in innovative theory building.

Gedo's investigations, based on his reports here of 50 fully completed analyses over a period of 25 years, have led to certain technical innovations which extend “beyond interpretation.” His clinical experiences have revealed “the omnipresence of archaic transferences, that is, of deficit states that invariably underlie the more manifest intrapsychic conflicts … One must often go ‘beyond insight’ to account for the effects of interventions intended to be interpretive.” The technical need to make interpretations “presupposes a shared language between the participant, the achievement of which usually requires lengthy preparation involving noninterpretive measures.”

Modern analytic practitioners will be at home with this statement and with many of Gedo's statements which I have chosen to highlight for this review.

Gedo finds that the extensive work of a generation of ego psychologists points inexorably to the fact that “resistances generally derive from archaic fixations that antedate the oedipal stage of development … Most of the ego defenses which serve to ward off oedipal strivings consist of behaviors that constitute, at the same time, adaptive solutions to the psychological vicissitudes of still earlier phases of development.”

In treatment, such cases require a symbiotic partner to sustain the enactments of the archaic transferences (by which Gedo means the “entire field of preoedipal derivatives”). Such patients have missing psychological aptitudes and skills. “The task of identifying psychological deficits, of bringing them to the attention of the analysand, and of assisting the latter in learning to function in the area of deficit, devolves primarily upon the analyst. These … operations [were] formerly designated parameters … [They are] essential but hitherto neglected aspects of analytic procedure.” A “holding environment” is required and the analyst must “enter into the patient's life as an auxiliary who can supply psychological skills unavailable when the analysand is left to his own devices.

Siamak Movahedi

Siamak Movahedi

Siamak Movahedi  

While this book is intended to serve as a guide to time-limited dynamic psychotherapy, I recommend it strongly to anyone who is interested in a clear and succinct blend of psychodynamic theory and clinical know-how.

After a brief overview and critical discussion of the history of short term psychotherapy, the authors get to the central point of their discussion, viz, time-limited dynamic psychotherapy (TLDP).

While dynamic focus may reflect any theoretical orientation, in TLDP, it is lodged within the interpersonal context. More specifically, it should capture “the salient pattern of interpersonal roles in which patients unconsciously cast themselves, the complementary roles in which they cast others, and the maladaptive interaction sequences, self-defeating expectations, and negative self-appraisals that result.” The function of a focus is to help the therapist assemble, sort, organize, and interpret the recurring patterns of interpersonal transactions in the therapy. In short, it is a blueprint for conducting the therapy.

For Strupp and Binder, interpretation remains the major mode of therapeutic encounter. However, they define it more liberally to include any timely and emotionally meaningful intervention. Thus, any affective communication, verbal or nonverbal, that facilitates an understanding of a current interpersonal conflict is thought of as interpretation.

Lucy Berman

Lucy Berman  

This new book by Giovacchini is divided into three parts, on psychic development and psychopathology, technique in the treatment of character disorders, and integration and adaptation in creative individuals.

126

Giovacchini describes character disorders as having defects in “the architecture of the personality” that are the outcome of faulty early development. To understand how psychopathology develops, we must examine the background of the caretaking interaction. The mother must be able to soothe her baby in order to feed him; in turn, the feeding experience causes the infant to feel further soothed. Many patients feel constantly agitated because they were not soothed as neonates; their incapacity to soothe themselves is a prominent feature of their psychopathology. Giovacchini describes a patient who began to feel calm when the analyst's capacity for soothing was internalized.

The analyst can foster a symbiotic transference that will rectify childhood deprivation. The mother's fusion can result in pathology when it is an engulfment based on her vulnerability and destructiveness rather than a smooth symbiotic union fostering an intuitive resonance, that enables her to be in immediate touch with her child's needs.

When the analyst merges with the patient based on his need to analyze and to foster autonomy and individuation, rather than on personal idiosyncratic needs, the analytic setting becomes a soothing environment, and through timely interpretations, the analyst provides symbolic nurture.

This comfortable state of fusion, however, is often achieved only after considerable turmoil, and the terrifying experience of having repeated in treatment the early traumatic maternal destructiveness. Giovacchini argues that psychopathology is better understood in terms of ego defects and structural factors than as the product of id forces clashing with the ego and the superego. He recalls several patients who defied all his efforts to understand their emotional problems in terms of inner conflict. He was formulating their problems in terms of higher psychic levels with psychological content. Rather, their difficulties originated in the earliest developmental stage which preceded psychological awareness. He was dealing with pre-mentational rather than mentational issues, and he found that he could not help these patients by making interpretations. He found that many of his patients are much too needy for the abstemious setting Freud recommended. They seek primitive gratification and demand that the analyst supply them with what they were deprived of during infancy. The silent analyst would not last beyond the first session.

Joan Cela

Joan Cela

Joan Cela  

The author presents an interesting approach to dream interpretation. This method relies on evidence of a “physical felt shift” in the body which must occur for an interpretation to be considered valid. If there has been no physical release in bodily feelings, then there is more interpretive work to be done. Only the dreamer can determine when his dream has been sufficiently understood and interpreted. With this understanding comes some freeing and loosening of energy which has been knotted and tied up inside the body and a physical release from tension occurs. Examples of a physical felt shift are freedom from global discomfort, heaviness, or jumpiness, and flushes or changes in breathing. This allows the energy to flow freely in the body.

The interpretation is arrived at by the dreamer learning to ask himself questions about himself and the dream. These are described in detail in the book. If nothing physical happens as a result of these questions, then the answers or interpretation that he has arrived at are not considered to be complete, or valid. The author wants the dreamer to bring something new to his awareness rather than repeat a variation of his same thoughts and feelings about himself. There are two stages in this method of dream interpretation. In the first stage, a “breakthrough” tells the dreamer what the dream is about. This information may be either old or new. In the second stage, new information is acquired which the dreamer uses for his own personal growth. This does not always happen, but is aimed for.

The author believes wholeheartedly that welcoming and enjoying the dream is more important than the actual interpretation. Not insight, but growth is the purpose for understanding a dream.

Should Analysts Love Their Patients?**

Robert Weinstein PHD

Robert Weinstein

41 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10023

Robert Weinstein   Graduate of the New York University post-Doctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis, has held staff and supervisory positions at The Neurological Institute, Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center, and New York Medical College. Currently, he is on the faculty of the Brooklyn Institute for Psychotherapy, and is an adjunct professor of clinical psychology at Union Graduate School. Dr. Weinstein is in private practice in New York City.

In 1926, on the occasion of Freud's seventieth birthday, Ferenczi wrote that psychoanalysis works through the deepening and enlargement of our knowledge, a task accomplished only through love. Thus, it is the analyst's love that ultimately heals the patient. What is surprising, then, in the sixty years that have passed, is how little has been written about the central and complex nature of love as it enters the analytic process. Far more has been written on the therapeutic uses of hate, about the analyst's rage, greed, grandiosity, competitiveness, despair and hopelessness than about his love. Although we as analysts are supposed to be experts on love, and the subject certainly fascinates all of us, Tauber (1979) addresses the current dilemma well when he writes, “I have thought for a long time that what strongly blocks us is a profound unease in dealing with love, affection and tenderness in our work; we have acknowledged the need to deal with anxiety, hate, rage, etc. but are unclear about and evasive with love, affection and tenderness…” Is Tina Turner speaking to the therapeutic community when she says “What's love got to do with it? Who needs a heart when a heart can be broken?”

Yet we are all therapists with hearts, and none of us would disagree with the importance of such aspects of love as positive regard, empathy, or understanding.

*This paper will appear in a forthcoming book entitled Love: Psychoanalytic Perspectives edited by Judith Lasky and Helen Silverman to be published by New York University Press.103

Estelle Borowitz

Estelle Borowitz

Estelle Borowitz  

Toni Bernay and Dorothy Cantor have edited an important book. This group of articles by contributors versed in both psychoanalytic concepts and contemporary insights into feminine psychology has been aptly subtitled “new psychoanalytic visions.” What becomes clear as “new” for women is the integration of aggression and sexuality in the construction of identity. Althea Horner notes in the foreword that women have been stereotyped as masochistic because they have been trained to “preserve the sense of self as good at all costs, fearful of the rage that lies on the other side of the split.” The current atmosphere—at least in the United States—offers “opportunity and choice as to how to live our one and only life when these two threads of our humanity can be woven together in harmony.”

In their introduction, Bernay and Cantor state their purpose to be that of working toward an “expanded perspective for understanding women,” one which “encompasses the female experience” rather than devalues it. The articles achieve that purpose.

The opening essay reassesses traditional ideas about femininity. Helen Block Lewis reviews Freud's contributions in the context of their historical discovery and their sexism, while also pointing to those of his ideas which have been useful and lasting contributions to women's liberation. She cites important modern anthropological evidence that would alter Freud's views regarding femininity.

In the second chapter, Eleanor Galenson reports on recent research into the sexual development of young girls.

The Psychotherapy Research Project, organized in 1954 at the Menninger Foundation, was designed to explore such fundamental questions as: How does psychoanalysis work? What factors produce, hinder, mediate change—factors in the patient, the therapist, their relationship, the patient's evolving life? It examines these questions by following the course of 42 lives in treatment, half of them in psychoanalysis and half in expressive and supportive psychoanalytic psychotherapy. The project involved 37 staff members at Menninger and 10 different consultants; it has already produced several books and monographs on, for example, the psychological testing done continuously over the life of the project, the role of situational variables as the program discovered them, and so on. Robert S. Wallerstein, one of the chairmen and principal investigators (others were Lewis Robbins and Otto Kernberg—the latter co-author of yet another monograph on this project), has now produced this comprehensive clinical casebook that describes these 42 cases (and lives) in rare detail. The organization of the book is by clinical question: under “The Analysis of the Hysterical Patient: Limitations?,” for example, are to be found, along with theoretical discussion, detailed accounts of the patients known as “The Adoptive Mother,” “The Tantrum Woman,” and “The Snake Phobia Woman.” Specific references to all three of these patients, however, also occur in many other places, as do less extensive references to several other cases in this chapter. There is a wonderfully detailed subject index over 14 large, close-set pages, a name index (to workers on this project and authorities) and a “Concordance of the Patients” showing the pages on which the full case description is given, followed by every page in which reference to that patient is made—as many as 72 other references, and as few as 20 (to “The Silent Woman,” perhaps unsurprisingly).

Lynn Perlman   Licensed clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst in private practice in Brookline and Newton Highlands, Massachusetts. She is on the faculty and is a supervisor at the Boston Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. She is a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis and the Massachusetts Psychological Association.

Introduction

In my preliminary attempts to understand the impact of an analyst's pregnancy on the conduct of a psychoanalysis, I encountered what first appeared to be an apparent lack of impact. This was evident in the sparsity of the literature. It is interesting to note that a topic such as this, with perhaps wide ranging implications for work with patients, had received little attention until the last fifteen years. When Ruth Lax (1969) wrote her article, “Some Considerations About Transference and Countertransference Manifestations Evoked by the Analyst's Pregnancy,” she could find only two articles pertaining to this topic. Why should this have been the case?

A second example of an apparent lack of interest comes from a personal experience. In the clinic at which I had been working, five of the therapists were either pregnant or had just had babies. In addition, two of the male therapists were hoping that their wives would become pregnant. The subject of the pregnant therapist was relevant to much of the work going on there, and I was asked to present some of the information I had gathered on the topic. The clinic had among its population of therapists ten males. Of these ten therapists, only one was present at my talk; and, significantly enough, his wife was a practicing midwife. The director of the clinic, a male psychiatrist (who also was not present), many years ago had written a paper on womb envy.

The Question of Termination In Modern Psychoanalysis**

Evelyn Liegner PHD

Evelyn Liegner

21 Cedar Drive
Great Neck, N.Y. 11201

Evelyn Liegner   Founder, Dean of Admissions, training analyst and supervisor at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and is a training analyst and supervisor at the Boston Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. She is a member of the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis and the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis and has served on the faculty of the California Graduate Institute and the Philadelphia School of Psychoanalysis. She has published clinical papers and has written on James Joyce and Walt Whitman. Her private practice is conducted in Great Neck, New York.

There is no reference to the topic of termination in the growing body of literature with a modern psychoanalytic perspective. Since the founding of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies in 1971, not one lecture, seminar, workshop, or course of study has had this subject as its focus. Nor to the best of my knowledge, have other institutes, identified with or closely related to the theoretical and therapeutic aims which can be subsumed under the category of Modern Freudian analysis, concerned themselves with this complex issue.

Yet the subject is an exceedingly multifaceted one. For when we speak of termination of analysis whom do we have in mind? Are we referring only to adults who may be classified as suffering from psychoneurotic conflicts, those readily amenable to classical analysis and interpretation? Such patients have become an almost extinct species as our knowledge, theoretical and clinical, compels us to recognize that whether it be our changing cultural values, child-rearing practices, or potential world-destruction threats, our practices now include children, adolescents, couples, families, and group members. Another separate category includes analysts and candidates of analytic institutes; it is time for us to discard the myth of their intrinsicallly superior mental health.

*For their invaluable comments on this article, I wish to thank Hyman Spotnitz and Leslie Rosenthal.5

Benjamin Margolis

239 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10024

Benjamin Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; adjunct professor at the Union Graduate School. Publications in psychoanalysis.

Joining is a powerful technique for resolving narcissistic resistance in psychoanalytic therapy. Its very power, however, calls for prudence in determining when and how to apply it. In the hands of the uninitiated, and used without reference to the larger maturational purpose which it aims to advance, joining, especially in its dystonic form, may subserve analytic aggrandizement against the patient; at worst, it may destroy the analysis. In this spirit, Spotnitz (1976) warns against using the joining technique as “a gimmick, a device that can be flicked on mechanically” (p. 42), and Nelson and Nelson (1957) similarly advise against “shotgun” application (p. 12).

The nucleus of therapy with the preoedipal patient is in the transference-countertransference relationship, reflected in the patient's evolving feelings toward the analyst and the latter's perception of the process through the medium of his own induced feelings. Generally speaking, technical skills such as joining come into perspective only as they further the objectives of a comprehensive therapeutic design associated with the patient-analyst relationship. The joining technique, powerful as it is, has no intrinsic significance. It is means to an end. Its value derives wholly from its role as handmaiden of a clinical method. If, therefore, we elect to study its many uses in treatment and to trace the sources of its effectiveness, we do so only in order to clarify how modern analysis goes about its pursuit of larger analytic goals.

*This paper evolved out of a series of summer workshops in modern psychoanalysis given by the author at the California Graduate Institute.19

Harold Stern

Harold Stern

Harold Stern  

This book adds considerably to the dimensions of our consciousness by informing us of the many facets of the concepts of evil which for most of us would not be at all evident. In her introduction, Marie Coleman Nelson cogently states, “Neither spiritual directives nor rational-ethical systems have succeeded in immunizing human beings against powerful inducements to destroy or to conspire in their own destruction. The more human beings learn about themselves and their universe, the more intent they seem to do away with both” (p. 11). The book is divided into three parts: Models and Origins, Therapeutic Encounters and Interdisciplinary Perspectives. It begins with Civilized Models of Evil by Vytautas Kavolis. Kavolis provides an interesting comparison of mythological, historical and religious origins of the concept of evil. He shows that the concept of evil comes from a process of rebellion against God's will, which is a basic model for moral good.

George Mora in “Reification of Evil: Witchcraft, Heresy, and the Scapegoat,” begins by stating that the concept of evil has been an intrinsic aspect of human existence from earliest times. He shows how women and minorities, such as Huguenots, Jews, and the mentally ill, can become victims of religious and racial persecution based upon pathological archaic distortions and projections.

E. Mansell Pattisen in “Psychoanalysis and the Concept of Evil,” argues that there are subtle, but profound shifts in our national attitudes from social to personal goals and from moral to biological goals. He questions Philip Rieff's contention that psychoanalysis is a science of morals.

One might say that Mrs. C and I fell in love. From the moment she walked into my office, it seemed as though she and I had been fated to meet, and that knowing each other was going to affect us profoundly. Our positive feelings for one another did not seem to be tempered by the mundane disappointments, fears, frustrations and miscommunications that pervade most relationships. Our relationship seemed free of earthly imperfections.

Even the idea that there would ever be a change from these blissful, halcyon days was far removed from our consciousness. We acted and felt with each other as though this perfect state of affairs would continue indefinitely. While all the rest of the world seemed to be floundering in a sea of discontent and disharmony, together we were safe, warm and calm.

Reason would have told me otherwise. Mrs. C had been referred to me as a terminally ill cancer patient. She had a cancer which medical science has no successful method of treating, and her prognosis gave her only one year to live. (Yet, she seemed to be the picture of health; it was not difficult for me to put out of my mind that our time together would, most likely, be extremely limited.)

Even beyond that, of course I knew that the state of being in love is a psychotic process. No relationship remains free for long of conflictual feelings. Hate and aggression, as well as love, are essential components of reality. In real-life relationships, the feeling of “being in love” is usually all too quickly replaced by a more realistic mutual understanding in which character flaws and limitations are able to be observed and tolerated.

73

Martin Gliserman

Martin Gliserman

Martin Gliserman  

Rejected by the mainstream, Lacan nonetheless has ardent followers as well as eager would-be readers and daunted interpreters, hence the growing number of “guides” to Lacan's writings. However one feels about Lacan, his ideas and his style, his insistence that we attend to Freud's concern with language and his own meditations on that concern make him a theorist worth knowing. The work of Muller and Richardson is dependably clarifying.

The writers of this guide note that Lacan's “message is locked up in an expression so obscure and enigmatic that for the uninitiated it constitutes a kind of rebus [as Freud once described the dream] in itself” (p. 2). The writers do a very good job of representing Lacan's seminal essays without pretending they understand everything—i.e., we often find phrases such as, “Lacan seems to mean …” In a way, the essays are translations, but they go beyond that by filling in important historical information, the context of Lacan's thinking (e.g., Levi-Strauss). For someone who has read Ecrits, the essays act as a kind of dialogue and a reinforcement of the conceptual field Lacan lays out. The writers also offer us, at the end of each chapter a “map of the text”—an outline which allows the reader to see the basic gestalt of the argument and the process thereof. There are, as well, notes on Lacan's notes for each chapter, and a lengthy bibliography.

The writers correctly say that Lacan's style is linked to his subject matter—“Lacan not only explicates the unconscious but strives to imitate it” (p. 3).

Freud drew attention to three major obstacles in working with narcississtic patients: indifference, hostility, and the absence of a coherent ego.

About indifference Freud (1917) says: “They manifest no transference and for that reason are inaccessible to our efforts.”

Freud (1912) writes of hostility: “Where the capacity for transference has become essentially limited to a negative order, as is the case with paranoics, there ceases to be any possibility of influence or cure.”

The absence of a coherent ego is an obstacle because analysis requires a strong ego. Freud (1940) says of the ego needed for analysis: “It must, however hard it may be pressed by the hostile powers, have retained a certain amount of coherence and some fragment of understanding for the demands of reality.”

In his final work, The Outline of Psychoanalysis, Freud (1940) regretfully concedes that psychoanalysis does not yet possess the techniques for working with narcissistic patients.

We must renounce the idea of trying our plan of cure upon psychotics—renounce it perhaps forever or perhaps only for the time being, till we have found some other plan better adapted for them. (p. 173)

Plans better adapted to them have dominated the psychoanalytic literature for several decades.

In the 1930s and 1940s Melanie Klein and Hyman Spotnitz were focussing on the aggressive side of Freud's dual drive theory.

[[RunningHead]]

The Management of Aggression in Modern Psychoanalytic Treatment**

Jacob Kirman PHD

Jacob Kirman

254 East 68 Street
New York, N.Y. 10021

Jacob Kirman   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and a Professor of Psychology at Queens College of CUNY. He is a training analyst, control analyst and a faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He is currently the chairman of the Education and Accreditation Committee of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis.

Human life is driven by two great forces: love and hate. As psychoanalysts, we must be concerned with both these forces—even though some of us may have a predilection for one or the other. Freud himself, though he eventually accorded aggression as much theoretical importance as the libidinal drive, never fully integrated the concept of aggression into his theory of analytic treatment, nor did he give it adequate recognition in his account of the severe psychopathologies he referred to as the narcissistic neuroses. The modern psychoanalytic movement begun over 30 years ago by Hyman Spotnitz, has attempted, among other things, to correct this imbalance. At a time when the schizophrenic patient was seen as suffering from excess anxiety and overmuch self love, Spotnitz recognized the central role of aggression and defenses against aggression in the treatment of such narcissistic disorders. The emphasis on aggression has been necessary because most people don't like being on the receiving end of aggression, nor is it easy to acknowledge it in ourselves. But it should be pointed out that modern analysts are not interested only in hate and aggression; they try to help patients feel, tolerate, and verbally express all of their feelings and impulses, including loving ones.

While different analytic schools disagree about the sources of human aggression, there is general agreement that it has both constructive and destructive aspects, and can be manifested either as destructive hatred or as self assertion.

*This is a revised version of a talk presented at the conference of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis on May 3, 1986.37

The Analysis of Defense: The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense Revisited. Joseph Sandler with Anna Freud. New York: International Universities Press, 1985. 556 pp.

Harold Davis

Harold Davis

Harold Davis  

This book is the outcome of a series of discussions between Anna Freud and the research group at the Hampstead Clinic over a year's time in 1972—73—36 years after the first publication of her classic work, The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense. The discussions (27 in all) focused on her book chapter by chapter, with at least one session devoted to each chapter. The author, Joseph Sandler, has organized the material into chapters with the same titles as those in the original book. He introduced each chapter with a summary of Anna Freud's chapter which he follows with edited transcriptions of the relevant discussions. As chair of the discussions Sandler acted as both spokesman for the research group and discussion leader. The result is that the discussions are largely a dialogue between Freud and Sandler. Sandler was editorin-chief of The International Journal of Psycho-Analysis and is now Sigmund Freud Professor of Psychoanalysis and director of The Sigmund Freud Center for Study and Research in Psychoanalysis at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
